O.outcome_detail: self-reported learning need regarding own strengths and weaknesses in communication

cells.quote: Regarding learning needs, a significant difference emerged in terms of a higher value in the group with data at T0 and T1 regarding one’s own strengths and weaknesses in communication (M=4.1 vs. 3.8, F(1.260)=3.99, p=.047).
cells.note: The contrast is a dropout analysis, not a treatment comparison.

O.outcome_detail: self-assessed confidence in taking a patient’s history

cells.quote: The self-assessments of the students’ own skills at T0 showed differences in the confidence in the ability to take a patient’s history (M=2.5 in the group with data for T0 and T1 vs. 2.2, F(1.264)=6.19, p=.013)
cells.note: The contrast is a dropout analysis, not a treatment comparison.

O.outcome_detail: self-assessed knowledge of how to disclose a diagnosis comprehensibly

cells.quote: The self-assessments of the students’ own skills at T0 showed differences in knowing how disclose a diagnosis in a comprehensible fashion (3.1 vs. 2.7, F(1,266)=11:43, p=.001)
cells.note: The contrast is a dropout analysis, not a treatment comparison.

O.outcome_detail: self-assessed confidence in disclosing a serious diagnosis

cells.quote: The self-assessments of the students’ own skills at T0 showed differences in the confidence in regard to actually disclosing a serious diagnosis (2.7 vs. 2.4, F(1.266)=4.63, p=.032).
cells.note: The contrast is a dropout analysis, not a treatment comparison.

D.comparison: extension principle, symbolic method, and 2-tuple CWW approaches

O.outcome_detail: uniqueness and uncertainty modeling of linguistic strategy recommendations

cells.quote: Also, through the c omparison of the recommendations generated by different CWW approaches, we found that Per-C outperforms the others CWW approaches by gener ating unique recommendations in 100% cases as well as modeling the word uncertainty in the best possible way , which other approaches failed to do.
cells.note: The study compares computational recommendations from CWW approaches; it does not report a randomized or other eligible experimental design, statistical test, or printed effect size.

O.outcome_detail: percentage passing the exam among students who took the exam

cells.quote: the percentage of students who passed the exam was 68.8 % in 2022 and 53.6 % in 2023 out of those students who took the exam.
cells.note: This sentence appears in the wiki entry but not in the supplied study text; the comparison is descriptive and no statistical test was reported.

O.outcome_detail: percentage passing the exam among all enrolled students

cells.quote: Referring to all students enrolled in the course, the percentages are 40.0 % (2022) and 31.5 % (2023).
cells.note: This sentence appears in the wiki entry but not in the supplied study text; the comparison is descriptive and no statistical test was reported.

D.treatment: academic research aligned with industry work

O.outcome_detail: reported alignment between academic research and current industry position

cells.quote: Of the 36 interviewees, 25 described alignment between their academic research and their current industry position.
cells.note: The study reports a thematic prevalence, not a causal comparison or measured outcome difference.

O.outcome_detail: German M2 examination accuracy

cells.quote: Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-5 Instant both correctly answered 289 (91.5%) questions, achieving an accuracy of 91.5% (95% CI 87.85%-94.06%) and committing 27 (8.5%) errors each.

O.outcome_detail: response latency

cells.quote: The Gemini 2.5 Flash model (mean 1.57, SD 1.06 s) was significantly faster than the GPT-5 Instant model (mean 2.07, SD 1.89 s).

O.outcome_detail: final German M2 examination accuracy after rescuing T1 errors

result.effect: Gemini system 94.3% (298/316) and GPT-5 system 95.6% (302/316) after rescue

cells.quote: Following the application of the 2-tiered rescue protocol, the final accuracy for the Gemini system (Flash and Pro) was 94.3% (298/316; 95% CI 91.18%-96.37%). The final accuracy for the GPT-5 system (Instant and Thinking) was 95.6% (302/316; 95% CI 92.70%-97.34%).

O.outcome_detail: odds of a correct model response

result.effect: Gemini OR 0.579 per 1-point increase; GPT-5 OR 0.523 per 1-point increase; both P<.001

cells.quote: For every 1-point increase on the 5-point difficulty scale, the odds of a correct T1 response decreased by 42.1% for Gemini Flash (odds ratio [OR] 0.579, 95% CI 0.425-0.788; P<.001) and by 47.7% for GPT-5 Instant (OR 0.523, 95% CI 0.379-0.720; P<.001).

O.outcome_detail: mean final grade across all school subjects at age 16

cells.quote: Both papers found significantly lower attainment of between 0.07 and 0.08 marks achieved by children with T1DM compared with their non-diabetic counterparts.
cells.note: Systematic review of two observational Swedish cohort studies; GRADE certainty was VERY LOW, and the cohorts overlapped.

O.outcome_detail: Mean attainment at compulsory-school testing

cells.quote: Those diagnosed aged 10–15 years were found to have 0.06 lower attainment, those diagnosed aged 5–9 years were found to have 0.07 lower attainment and those diagnosed aged 0–4 years were found to have 0.15 lower attainment.
cells.note: The review reports this association from Persson et al, using those without diabetes as the reference group.

O.outcome_detail: Sports/Athletics grade attainment at age 16

cells.quote: In Sports/Athletics, children with T1DM were found to be more likely to achieve lower grades and less likely to achieve higher grades.
cells.note: Narrative synthesis of two observational Swedish cohort studies.

O.outcome_detail: Maths grade attainment at age 16

cells.quote: In Maths and Swedish, children with T1DM had a higher odds of a low score (no clear differences for high scores), and there were no clear effects for English.
cells.note: The synthesis reports a negative association for lower Maths grades, while high-grade differences were unclear.

O.outcome_detail: Swedish grade attainment at age 16

cells.quote: In Maths and Swedish, children with T1DM had a higher odds of a low score (no clear differences for high scores), and there were no clear effects for English.
cells.note: The synthesis reports a negative association for lower Swedish grades, while high-grade differences were unclear.

O.outcome_detail: English grade attainment at age 16

cells.quote: In Maths and Swedish, children with T1DM had a higher odds of a low score (no clear differences for high scores), and there were no clear effects for English.
cells.note: The review reports no clear English effects in Dahlquist and Källén, but states that Persson et al showed a similar, weaker pattern.

O.outcome_detail: mean final grade at age 16, examined across attainment quantiles

result.effect: Negative effect greatest in the lowest quantile, diminishing with increasing attainment quantiles, and statistically insignificant for the highest attaining quantile

cells.quote: Quantile regression—negative effect of T1DM greatest in the lowest quantile of attainment, diminishing with increasing attainment quantiles, becoming statistically insignificant for the highest attaining quantile.
cells.note: The review reports this quantile-regression result from Persson et al., one of two included Swedish electronic population cohort studies.

O.outcome_detail: school attendance

result.effect: 2.6% lower attendance in year 3 to 3.4% lower attendance in year 5; p<0.001

cells.quote: In an excluded study, Cooper et al 7 showed significantly lower school attendance in children with type 1 diabetes in all age groups (p<0.001); from 2.6% lower attendance in year 3 up to 3.4% lower attendance in year 5.
cells.note: This attendance finding was reported second-hand from an excluded study; neither included study assessed school attendance.
